newsitem.title: USA: Norfolk seeks Conrail lockout injunction.
newsitem.headline: Norfolk seeks Conrail lockout injunction.

text.p: Norfolk Southern Corp on Thursday filed a motion in U.S. federal court for a preliminary injunction against the so-called "lock-out" provision of the amended merger agreement between CSX Corp and Conrail Inc, according to court papers.

It also asked the U.S. District Court in Philadelphia for a partial summary judgment on the number of shares owned by CSX and those acting in concert with it. Norfolk contends CSX already owns more than 20 percent of Conrail's shares, making it "an interested shareholder," according to papers.

CSX amended its $8.5 billion friendly cash and stock merger pact with Conrail in December, to give Conrail holders another $870 million, or $9.3 billion. They also revised the deal to prohibit either company from entering an agreement with a third party before 1999. The previous agreement set a July 1997 date.

Hours later, rival bidder Norfolk Southern increased its all cash offer for all of Conrail's outstanding common shares to $115 per share, or $10.5 billion, from its previous rejected bid of $110 per share. It said it would challenge the legality of the provision that extended the lock-out period.

At the time, Norfolk said the U.S. District Court agreed to consider if CSX owned 20 percent of Conrail shares. That would require CSX to pay all Conrail shareholers $110 per share in cash under Pennsylvania's Fair Value Statute, it said.
CSX had previously bought 19.9 percent of Conrail in a cash tender offer at $110 per share. But it is now offering Conrail shareholders a combination of cash and stock worth about $102 per share.
Even though Norfolk's bid has been higher during the takeover fight, Conrail contends the union with CSX would be a better fit.
Norfolk said the value of CSX's proposed offer depended on the price of CSX stock at some point in the future. Neither Conrail nor CSX officials were immediately available to comment.
In court papers, Norfolk said the extended lock-out period was an attempt to disenfranchise Conrail shareholders.

"In addition to being 'fundamentally unfair' in that it effectively disenfranchises Conrail shareholders by depriving them of meaningful choice, the two-year lock-out period impermissibly binds the hands of future Conrail directors and is an abdication by Conrail directors of their fiduciary duties," the papers said.
